stimulus.title: Height of a weight on a spring
stimulus.html: A weight hangs from a spring above a floor. The weight is pulled and released, and then it bobs up and down with a frequency of 0.5 cycle per second. The bottom of the weight is 60 centimeters above the floor at its highest and 40 centimeters above the floor at its lowest. At time t=0t = 0 seconds, the weight is at its highest. The sinusoidal function hh models the height of the bottom of the weight above the floor, in centimeters, at time tt. The graph of hh for one cycle is shown with its axes unscaled. The points FF, GG, JJ, KK and MM are on the graph: FF and MM are highest points, JJ is a lowest point, and GG and KK are on the midline.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of the points FF, GG, JJ, KK and MM.

rubric.point: The extremes: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>60</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F = (0, 60)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>40</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J = (1, 40)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>60</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M = (2, 60)</annotation></semantics></math>

The midline points: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G = (0.5, 50)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K = (1.5, 50)</annotation></semantics></math>

parts.sample: A frequency of 0.5 cycle per second means a period of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>0.5</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{0.5} = 2</annotation></semantics></math> seconds, so the points are <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{2}{4} = 0.5</annotation></semantics></math> second apart. The midline is <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{60 + 40}{2} = 50</annotation></semantics></math>. <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>60</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F = (0, 60)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G = (0.5, 50)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>40</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J = (1, 40)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K = (1.5, 50)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>60</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M = (2, 60)</annotation></semantics></math>.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: The function hh is given by h(t)h(t)=asin⁡(b(t+c))+d= a\sin(b(t + c)) + d, where aa, bb, cc and dd are constants. Find values of aa, bb, cc and dd.

rubric.point: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b = \pi</annotation></semantics></math> (from the period 2 seconds) and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d = 50</annotation></semantics></math>

<math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math> and <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> that fit the graph: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a = 10</annotation></semantics></math> with <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c = \frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, or <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a = -10</annotation></semantics></math> with <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c = -\frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>
accept: any <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math> that differs from these by a multiple of 2

parts.sample: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d = 50</annotation></semantics></math> and the amplitude is <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{60 - 40}{2} = 10</annotation></semantics></math>. The period is <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>0.5</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1}{0.5} = 2</annotation></semantics></math> seconds (not 0.5), so <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>π</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b = \frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi</annotation></semantics></math>. With <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a = 10</annotation></semantics></math>, the sine pattern starts (midline, rising) at <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t = 1.5</annotation></semantics></math>, or one period earlier at <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t = -0.5</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c = \frac{1}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(t)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 10\sin\left(\pi\left(t + \frac{1}{2}\right)\right) + 50</annotation></semantics></math>. Check: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(0)</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>10</mn><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 10\sin\frac{\pi}{2} + 50</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= 60</annotation></semantics></math>.

parts.label: C(i)
parts.prompt: Is hh increasing or decreasing on the interval (0.5,1)(0.5, 1)? Give a reason for your answer in the context of the problem.

rubric.point: Decreasing, with a reason: on <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0.5, 1)</annotation></semantics></math> the weight moves from the midline height down to its lowest point <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math>
accept: the weight is moving down, from 50 cm to 40 cm

parts.sample: <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is decreasing on <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0.5, 1)</annotation></semantics></math>: the weight is moving down, from 50 cm above the floor at <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t = 0.5</annotation></semantics></math> to its lowest height, 40 cm, at <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t = 1</annotation></semantics></math>.

parts.label: C(ii)
parts.prompt: Is the graph of hh concave up or concave down on the interval (0.5,1)(0.5, 1), and is the rate of change of hh increasing or decreasing there? Explain your reasoning.

rubric.point: Concave up and the rate of change of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is increasing, with a reason: the graph is below its midline, bending up toward the lowest point <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>J</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math>, where the weight momentarily stops
accept: the weight slows down as it nears the bottom, so the negative rate of change increases toward 0

parts.sample: The graph of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is concave up on <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0.5, 1)</annotation></semantics></math>, so the rate of change of <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is increasing. The weight is moving down but slowing as it nears the bottom: the rate of change is negative and rises toward 0 at <math class="pcalc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t = 1</annotation></semantics></math>.
